BOPEN.heard: Building virtual environments exam prep, key terms, the blender interface and modeling. 30 terms for modeling a game asset in blender, from the parts of the window to meshes, transforms, modifiers and materials. The exact term lets you tell an AI coding agent precisely what to change.

BIDEA.heard: Hollow, this is Liam in for bear. Newcomers often say an object's scale is its size, it is not. Scale is a multiplier left on the object and size is the real dimensions you end up with. A pole can look right and still be a 2 meter cube wearing a small scale. This film goes through the blender terms, each one shown, so you can name the exact one.

BDEFS.heard: Six labels sit in the corners of the pictures that follow. In the book text, the course text uses and explains the term. In the glossary, the term is on the course term list, but the text does not explain it. Editor or docs, the term comes from the editor itself or its official documentation. Computed, the numbers are worked out on screen from stated inputs. Illustrative data, numbers chosen to show the idea not measured, conceptual, a drawing of the idea. With no data behind it.

B0101.heard: This table is the map, 30 terms for modeling a game asset in Blender by hand or through the Blender MCP, the model context protocol Lincoln Agent uses. First the Blender window, 3D viewport, outliner, properties editor, timeline, workspace, object mode, edit mode and collection.

B0102.heard: The second group is Mesh Anatomy. Mesh, Vertex, Edge, Face, Quad, Polygon, Count, Normal, and Flip normals. These terms say what a model is made of and how it is counted.

B0103.heard: The third group is placing and measuring. Transform, origin, pivot, apply transforms, local and global space, unit and right-handed, plus Z up. These terms say where a model sits, how big it is and which way is up.

B0104.heard: The fourth group is shaping and surfacing. Modifier, mirror, subdivision surface, bevel, UV map, named for the U and V axis of an image, unwrapping, and material versus texture. These terms say how a model is built faster and how it gets its look.

B0201.heard: This is a drawing of the Blender window cut into four areas. The 3D viewport lit in red on the left is the area where you look at the scene in three dimensions and edit it. Here a cube turns inside it. Every other area shows or changes something about what you see there. For example, to start the Blender MCP connection by hand, you press N in the 3D viewport and open the MCP for Blender tab.

B0202.heard: The Outliner at the top right is a tree that lists every object and collection in the scene. Here it lists three objects in one collection, cube, camera and light, and cube is selected. Click a name and that object is selected. For example, after an agent's script builds a checkpoint post for a platformer, the Outliner lists its base, its pole, its pennant, and its collision hull by name, so you can see that each part exists.

B0203.heard: The Properties Editor below it holds tabs of settings for whichever object is selected, such as its Transform, its modifiers, and its material. With the cube selected, it shows the cube's location 0, 0, and 1 meter. The Outliner lists what is in the scene, and the Properties Editor shows the settings of one selected thing. For example, select the pennant of a checkpoint post, and the Properties Editor shows which material it uses and lets you change it.

B0301.heard: Five tabs sit across the top of this simplified blender window. A workspace is a saved arrangement of editors for one job picked from those tabs. The tabs change which editors you see not the scene. Here the tabs light and turn and stop on animation with three editors on screen. For example, to lay out the image on a crate you switch to the UV editing workspace and to set up its material you switch to shading and the crate itself never changes.

B0302.heard: The timeline holds the playback controls and a frame scale with keyframes marked as diamonds. Here keyframes at frames 1, 30 and 60 move the red block from 0 to 4 meters along a rail and back. The values between keys are worked out for you. A workspace decides which editors you see and the timeline is about frames and playback. For example, a coin that Bob's above a platform can be three keyframes on its height, played on the timeline.

B0401.heard: A cube glides across the view. In object mode you work on whole objects. You move, rotate and scale them, and the mesh inside is not touched. Here one move carries all eight vertices together, 5.9 units, and only the cube's location changes. For example, in object mode you lift a finished crate onto a platform, and its shape stays exactly as you built it.

B0402.heard: Edit Mode opens the mesh itself so you work on its vertices, edges, and faces. Here one vertex, the red dot, is pulled up and the other seven stay. The shape changes and the object's location does not. Object Mode treats the cube as one thing and Edit Mode treats it as eight points. For example, to give a crate a sloping lid, you enter Edit Mode and raise the vertices along one side of its top.

B0403.heard: A collection is a named group of objects that you can hide, show, or export together. Here props holds the post and the pennant, and level holds the floor, the wall, and the lamp. Hiding level hides all three at once, so two of five objects stay visible. For example, keep a checkpoint post and its pennant in one collection, so you can export just that prop for Go-Doh without the test floor around it.

B0501.heard: A plain cube drawn solid, a mesh is the set of vertices, edges, and faces that make a 3D shape. It is the shape's points, lines, and surfaces, and it carries the model's real size. For example, a checkpoint post built for a platformer is made of separate meshes for its base, its pole, and its pennant, plus a simple box mesh that Go-Doh turns into collision.

B0502.heard: Now each corner turns red. A vertex is a corner point of a mesh, one position in space. Every corner of the cube is one vertex, eight in all. A vertex is a point and an edge is aligned between two points. For example, the far corner of the flat pen on a checkpoint post is one vertex and moving it in edit mode changes the pen in shape.

B0503.heard: Red lines now join the dots, and edge is a line joining two vertices. Counted once each, the cube has 12, and each one is shared by two faces. For example, the line where the top of a stair step meets its front where the player's foot lands is one edge of the steps mesh.

B0504.heard: The sides are tinted now. A face is a flat surface bounded by edges, the part that is filled in and drawn. The cube has six. For any close shape with no holes, vertices minus edges plus faces is two. Eight minus twelve plus six is two, and a prism gives two as well. For example, an agent building a pendant once failed with the error face already exists because it laid a back face over the same vertices as the front one.

B0601.heard: A square splits along a diagonal into two triangles. A quad is a face with four vertices. The GPU, the graphics processor, draws only triangles, so each quad is split in two. The cube's six quads become 12 triangles. For example, a floor tile under the player in a platformer can be modeled as one quad, and the engine draws it as two triangles.

B0602.heard: Four bars, four tallies of the same cube. Polygon count is not one number. Blender shows six faces. The engine budgets by triangles 12. Blender counts eight vertices, but the GPU splits a vertex wherever its faces need different normals or UVs, so this hard-edged cube needs 24. Face count is what Blender shows, and triangle count is what the engine budgets. For example, if a prop must stay under a triangle budget. Ask the agent for its triangle count, not its face count.

B0701.heard: A ring of 12 faces each with an arrow and light from the upper left. A normal is the direction a surface faces, the arrow out of the face. Lighting uses it and so does culling which skips faces that point away from the camera. Faces turned toward the light are bright, 6 of 12 here. For example, a checkpoint post's pennant is a single face, so it's normal points out of one side and you check it still shows from the other.

B0702.heard: Three arrows turn red and point inward. Flip normals are faces whose normals point into the shape so they face away from the light. They look dark or are not drawn at all. Here three are flipped and only three of twelve faces are still lit. A normal says which way a face points and a flipped one points inward. For example, if one side of a crate shows in go-dough as a black patch or a see-through hole, check for flipped normals.

B0801.heard: A square on a grid seen from above, transform means three things on an object. Location is where it is, rotation is how it is turned, and scale is how much it is stretched. Here the square moves to 3.1.5 turns 45 degrees and grows by 1.6. The mesh itself is not touched, for example placing a coin above a platform, tilting it, and making it a little bigger changes only the coins transform.

B0802.heard: Two posts each 1.8 meters placed at height zero. The origin is the point and objects, position, and rotation are measured from. On the left the origin is in the middle, so half the post sinks into the floor to minus 0.9 meters. On the right the origin is at the base and the post stands on the floor. For example the platformer's checkpoint post has its origin under the center of its base, so it stands where it is placed.

B0803.heard: A bar two units long turns 60 degrees two ways. A pivot is the point an object rotates and scales around. Turned about its middle, the tip moves a little. Turned about its end like a hinge, it swings far out to 1, 1.7. The origin is where an object is measured from, and the pivot is what a turn happens around. For example, a door in a level should swing on a pivot at its hinge edge, not at its center.

B0901.heard: Table of a pole's numbers. Apply transforms makes the object's rotation and scale into the mesh and resets them to neutral. This pole is a 2-meter cube scaled to 0.1, 0.1, 0.9. After apply, the scale reads 111 and the mesh is 1.8 meters tall. Scale is a multiplier and size is the real dimensions. For example, apply a pole's scale before export so a collider built from it is not stretched.

B0902.heard: A parent-shaped turns on a grid. Local and global space are two ways to give one point's position. Local coordinates are measured from the object's own origin, global ones from the scenes. As the parent turns, the red point stays at local 1, 0.5, while its global position becomes 4.12, 3.43. For example, a coin riding on a moving platform keeps its local position on it. While its global position changes as the platform travels.

B1001.heard: A player in a post side by side. The unit is the length one coordinate step stands for, usually a meter. In Blender, in GLTF, the GL transmission format and in Go-Doh, one unit is one meter, so nothing converts. The dashed post is 1.8 units beside the 2.1 meter player. In this made-up wrong case, take a unit as a centimeter and the post nearly vanishes, for example. A crate-modeled one unit tall arrives in Go-Doh, one meter tall.

B1002.heard: Blender's axis beside Godos, right-handed plus C up is how Blender sets its axis. Right-handed means X cross Y gives Z and in Blender Z points up. Godo is right-handed too but puts plus Y up as GLTF does. The exporter's plus Y up option moves the post's 1.8 Z extent on a Godos Y so it stands. For example, a checkpoint post is tall along Blender Z and if it arrives lying on its side in Godo. The plus Y up option was off.

B1101.heard: A base mesh, a modifier, and a result. A modifier is a live step that changes a mesh without editing it. Here it is subdivision surface at level 1. The base cube has 8 vertices and 6 faces, and the result has 26 and 24. Switch it off and the base is back. A modifier stays live and apply bakes its result in. For example, an agent exporting a checkpoint post can be told to apply modifiers, so Godo gets the finished shape.

B1102.heard: Now half a shape beside a dashed line. The mirror modifier cop is the mesh across an axis, so you model only one half. Here you place five vertices on the right, and the mirror across the line x equals zero makes a shape with eight. Edit one side and the other always matches. For example, model the left half of a robot enemy's head, and the mirror modifier keeps the right half identical while you work.

B1103.heard: One face is outline gains corners at each level. Subdivision surface is a modifier that splits faces and smooths them, and on an all-quad mesh each level makes four times as many faces. On the cube that is sixth and twenty-four, then ninety-six, watch the triangle budget. For example, a rounded boulder for level can start as a cube with subdivision surface on top, set to the lowest level that still looks smooth.

B1104.heard: Four squares from sharp to round, bevel turns a sharp edge or corner into a small slanted or rounded one. A sharp edge has no width so it cannot catch a highlight. Here the square has four vertices when sharp, then eight, twelve and sixteen as the bevel goes from one segment to three. More segments give a rounder edge and more vertices. For example, bevel the edges of a crate little, so the light in the game catches its corners.

B1201.heard: A cube beside a cross of six cells. A UV map is the flattened two-d layout of a mesh used to place a texture. You and V are the two axes of the image. Each numbered face has a matching cell where it reads the texture. A UV map is the flat layout and a material is the whole surface recipe. For example, the UV map of a crate decides which part of a wood image lands on its lid and which on its sides.

B1202.heard: The faces fly off the cube and lie flat. Unwrapping is cutting a mesh along seams and flattening it into a UV map. The red lines are the seams, the cuts. The cube has 12 edges and laid out as a cross, 5 stay joined and 7 are cut. For example, to unwrap a barrel for a level, you cut a seam down its side and around each end so the body lies flat as one strip.

B1203.heard: Material card beside a checker image, material versus texture. Material is the full surface recipe, its base color, how metallic it is and how rough. A texture is one image the material can read here filling the base color slot. One material can use no texture, one or many, and these values are only illustrative. For example, the checkpoint post uses a material named postmetal for its base and pole and flagcloth for its pennant. And either could read a texture or none.

B1301.heard: Look alike pairs side by side. The origin is the object's own point where its position and rotation are measured from. The pivot is the point a turn or stretch happens around. Here the pivot is set to a corner so the square swings about that corner.

B1302.heard: Scale is a multiplier left on the object, here's 0.5 while the mesh is still 2 meters. Size is the real dimensions you end up with. Scale times mesh gives what you see 1 meter. Apply transforms moves that size into the mesh.

B1303.heard: Face count is what Blender shows, six faces for the cube. Triangle count is what the engine budgets, 12 triangles because each quad is drawn as two. Compare models by the count the budget uses.

B1304.heard: A material is the whole surface recipe, its color, roughness, metal, and the rest. A texture is one image the recipe can use, a picture, and nothing more. Swap the texture and the recipe stays the same.

B1401.heard: Five vague requests to an agent driving blender each made exact. Make it smoother becomes at a subdivision surface modifier at level two. The chart shows the faces go from 6 to 24 to 96.

B1402.heard: I only want a model half becomes add a mirror modifier on X and model 5 vertices. The shape has 8, so you place 38% fewer.

B1403.heard: It lies on its side and Godot becomes Export GLTF with plus Y up, so blenders the extent of 1.8 meters lands on Godot's Y. Without it the post is 0.2 meters tall, with it 1.8.

B1404.heard: The scale is wrong becomes selected, then object, apply rotation and scale. The scale goes from 0.1, 0.1, 0.9 to 1, 1, 1. The mesh height drops from 2 meters to 1.8 and the size you see stays the same.

B1405.heard: The model is too heavy becomes look at the triangle count, then lower the subdivision level. Each level quadruples the triangles. Level 3 is 768 triangles and level 1 is 48.

B1501.heard: This is a checklist of six questions to ask before you hand a model to the game. First, is the origin where you want to place it, such as at the base of a post so it stands on the floor.

B1502.heard: Second is the scene in meters with a unit scale of 1.0, so that one unit means 1 meter in blender, in GLTF and in GoDo.

B1503.heard: Third is the transform applied, so the scale reads 1111. A scale left on the object is carried into anything built from its mesh, such as a collider.

B1504.heard: Fourth, do all normals point out so no face looks dark or goes missing. A flipped normal turns its face away from the light.

B1505.heard: Fifth is the triangle count within budget after the modifiers run. Each subdivision level multiplies the triangles, so count them after the modifiers, not before.

B1506.heard: Sixth is it unwrapped and does each material have the name the game expects, then say it exactly. Not fix the scale but apply rotation and scale, then check it reads 111.

BVDT.heard: Let's recap the 3D viewport shows the scene and the outliner lists what is in it. Object mode moves whole objects and edit mode changes the mesh itself. Engine's budget by triangles while Blender shows the face count. The origin is where an object is measured from the pivot when it turns around. Apply transforms so the mesh carries the real size and scale reads 111. Material is the whole surface recipe. And a texture is one image it uses.

BHTF.heard: Quizmy on Blender Modeling terms with short game-making cases one at a time. Use the terms Object Mode, Edit Mode, Origin, Pivot, Apply Transforms, Face Count, Triangle Count, Modifier, Material and Texture. For each case I must name the exact term and say why its look alike is wrong. Hold back the answer until I reply, then tell me whether I was right.

BOUT.heard: Key terms the Blender interface in modeling at Nick Bear Brown.
